title: Canada Weighs Winding Down 41-Year Kanishka Bombing Probe, Drawing Anguish From Victims' Families
excerpt: The RCMP briefed victims' families on plans to scale back the investigation into the 1985 Air India bombing; families have written to PM Mark Carney demanding the probe be renewed, not retired.
body:
• The RCMP briefed victims' families at a Toronto meeting on September 12 that it may scale back the task force investigating the 1985 Kanishka bombing and place the 41-year-old case in "inactive" status — the first official family briefing in 20 years.
  • Sanjay Lazar, chairman of the Kanishka Foundation, who lost his father, mother and infant sister in the attack, wrote to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney opposing any wind-down and demanding a renewed public appeal and a larger reward.
  • Air India Flight 182 was destroyed by a bomb over the Atlantic on June 23, 1985, killing all 329 aboard, including 268 Canadians — Canada's deadliest terrorist attack.
  • Families say they were told the burden of generating fresh leads would now fall on them, a proposal that has drawn anger and accusations that the authorities are surrendering.

Four decades after Air India Flight 182 — the Kanishka — was destroyed by a bomb over the Atlantic, Canadian authorities may be preparing to effectively end the active investigation, a move that has left victims' families furious. According to NDTV, which accessed details of a meeting organised at the request of RCMP top brass earlier this month, relatives were briefed about a possible decision to reduce the investigation task force and place the case in an "inactive" status.

The Toronto briefing on September 12 was the first official family meeting in 20 years, according to Sanjay Lazar, chairman of the Kanishka Foundation. What families heard has stunned them: after more than 40 years of waiting for justice, the investigation that Canadian authorities call the country's worst terrorist case could be quietly wound down.

"I was orphaned as a teenager"

Lazar, who lost his father, mother and infant sister in the bombing, wrote an urgent letter to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, copied to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, opposing any move to wind down the task force.

"I was orphaned as a teenager, when I lost my entire family...on 23rd June, 1985."

— Sanjay Lazar, Chairman, Kanishka Foundation, in a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney

"As the son of my late parents, and the last surviving member of that family, I feel duty bound to express my disgust, hurt and anger at the expressed intention of the RCMP to wind down the Air India Bombing investigations, and reject it," Lazar wrote, vowing to do "everything in my power to ensure that the search for the killers of the 'world's worst aviation bombing AI-182 Kanishka' is not given up."

Lazar also alleged "serious lapses and strange and highly questionable, dubious actions" during the investigation, including missing evidence and deleted surveillance recordings, and said witnesses connected to the case had been killed, threatened or otherwise lost over the years.

The deadliest attack in Canadian history

On June 23, 1985, Air India Flight 182, operating on the Montreal–London–Delhi route, exploded midair over the Atlantic off the Irish coast. All 329 people aboard the Boeing 747 were killed — 268 Canadian citizens, largely of Indian origin, 27 British citizens, 22 American citizens and 24 Indian citizens, including 82 children under the age of 13, according to the High Commission of India's statement on the 40th anniversary. The same day, a second bomb linked to the same conspiracy exploded at Tokyo's Narita airport, killing two baggage handlers.

The conspiracy was conceived, planned and executed in Canada by Khalistani extremists, and the bombing remains the deadliest terrorist attack in Canadian history and one of the worst aviation disasters ever. In 2006, the Canadian government appointed a Commission of Inquiry headed by former Supreme Court Justice John Major; its 2010 final report, "Air India Flight 182: A Canadian Tragedy," was a damning indictment of intelligence and law-enforcement failures before and after the attack, including the treatment of victims' families.

"Find another way rather than surrender"

What has angered families most is the suggestion, conveyed at the briefing, that the burden of generating fresh leads should now fall on the bereaved themselves. Lazar called on authorities to launch a renewed public appeal and to increase the $1-million reward offered for information leading to the perpetrators.

"If the current team cannot make progress, authorities must find another way rather than surrender."

— Sanjay Lazar, Chairman, Kanishka Foundation

A wound that still bleeds into diplomacy

The families' campaign has unfolded against a tense backdrop: India–Canada relations remain strained over Ottawa's handling of Khalistani separatist activity on Canadian soil, and the bombing — conceived in Canada, devastating mostly Canadians — sits at the emotional centre of that dispute. A 2023 Angus Reid poll found many Canadians have little to no knowledge of the attack, a fact that continues to frustrate relatives. Families have been working with the RCMP on returning victims' belongings and hope to display recovered wreckage in a museum.

What's next

All eyes are now on Prime Minister Mark Carney's response to Lazar's letter. Families are demanding that the investigation be renewed rather than retired: a larger task force, a fresh public appeal and a bigger reward. For relatives who have waited 41 years, an "inactive" stamp would feel, in Lazar's words, like surrender — and an end to the search for accountability in Canada's deadliest mass murder.
